title: Adaptive output quarantine and client surface proposal
body:
Purpose
This is a working PRD sketch proposing an 'adaptive output quarantine' layer for the Hosted API streaming surface. The goal: provide an explicit, low-friction mechanism for the server to hold, validate, and progressively commit structured or tool-invocation output to clients in a way that improves safety, developer ergonomics, and client-side UX for intermittent networks or low-bandwidth devices.

Motivation / problem statements
- Structured outputs and tool calls are increasingly interleaved with streaming text; current streams expose partial frames immediately or drop partials on network issues, leaving clients to implement brittle heuristics.
- We see three classes of failure modes: (1) early/incorrect structured fragments that break client JSON parsers, (2) tool-outputs that require server-side post-processing/validation before being safe to surface, (3) mobile/edge clients with sporadic connectivity that need compact checkpoints instead of long-running optimistic states.
- Existing approaches (immediate partial frames + resume tokens) push complexity to SDKs and customers. We can reduce engineer burden by defining a compact server-controlled quarantine lifecycle that clients can opt into.

High level proposal
- Introduce quarantined frames: server emits a quarantined frame when it has candidate structured output or a tool-call result that is not yet fully validated/committed. Quarantined frames are stable, checksumed blobs attached with a small metadata header (frame_id, schema_hint, confidence_score).
- Clients receive quarantined frames as part of the stream but must not treat them as authoritative until a subsequent commit frame is received.
- Commit frames: the runtime will emit a commit event for a quarantined frame when validation, downstream tool handshake, or other checks complete. Commit replaces the quarantined blob with a canonical output. Commit events contain a diff/patch or a replacement payload (depending on size).
- Timeout / fallback: if a quarantined frame does not receive a commit within a configurable SLA window (per-request or per-tenant), the runtime will emit a fallback frame which either (a) downgrades to a best-effort textual summary, or (b) emits a sanitized minimal response. This behavior is configurable by client via request-level flags.

API surface changes (draft)
- New events in streaming protocol (and same names mirrored in SDKs):
  - quarantined_frame: {frame_id, kind, schema_hint, length, checksum, confidence_score} (sent inline or as compact reference)
  - commit_frame: {frame_id, outcome: replaced|patched|validated, patch_checksum, final_payload_reference}
  - quarantine_timeout: {frame_id, policy: downgrade|sanitize, reason}
- Non-streaming / sync: follow-up commit metadata available via GET /responses/{response_id}/frames to poll commit state for previously returned quarantined frames.
- Request flags (SDK-friendly):
  - accept_quarantine: boolean (default true) — opt into the lifecycle.
  - quarantine_timeout_ms: integer — override default SLA.
  - fallback_policy: string — one of [downgrade_text, minimal_sanitize, blocked]
  - prefer_patch_commits: boolean — server should prefer patch diffs where possible to save bandwidth.

SDK ergonomics notes (web, mobile, server)
- Default SDK behavior: surface quarantined frames to application layer via an event (onQuarantineCandidate). SDKs must mark these as non-authoritative in generated transcripts. Use case: show a lightweight placeholder card in UI with a spinner and unobtrusive label "verifying..."
- Commit handling: SDK provides an onCommit(frame_id, payload, metadata) event. SDK will reconcile the transcript, applying patch or replacement atomically. Provide a small optimistic merge helper: if client already showed a placeholder card, patch in final content with a fade-in animation (web) or list item update (mobile).
- Offline/resume: SDK should persist a compact checkpoint including frame_ids and checksums. On resume, SDK asks server for commit states and reconciles. If commit not arrived, SDK can either (a) continue to show placeholder, (b) request explicit fallback via REST call.
- Developer ergonomics: provide a typed client helper to declare expected schema types and validators in client code (lightweight runtime validators) so client-side UI can do cheap early checks. Not mandatory but recommended for rich clients.

Server runtime considerations
- Quarantine store: small ephemeral store (in-memory with bounded TTL) for quarantined payloads keyed by frame_id, sharded by request_id. Metrics: size, time-to-commit, commit rate, fallback rate.
- Validation pipeline: pluggable steps (schema validation, tool handshake confirmation, info-flow safety checks) that can mark a quarantined frame as committed or rejected. Each step emits telemetry which maps to client-visible confidence_score updates.
- Cost model: quarantined frames increase memory pressure and potentially storage egress if patched multiple times. Default policy uses patch diffs to reduce resend size. Billing implications: commits and quarantine storage should be included in token/egress accounting; propose a small per-frame surcharge for quarantined frames over baseline to reflect resource cost — requires legal/pricing review.

Telemetry and observability
- New telemetry fields: frame_id, initial_confidence, time_to_commit_ms, commit_outcome, fallback_policy_used, schema_hint_score. Add traces mapping from request -> quarantined_frame -> commit outcome to help debugging regressions. Expose a per-route dashboard in Console showing quarantine load and failure patterns.

Example event sequence (streaming)
1) client starts streaming gen with accept_quarantine=true
2) server emits: text chunk A
3) server emits: quarantined_frame(frame_42, kind=tool_result, schema_hint=payment_receipt, confidence=0.62)
4) client shows placeholder card for frame_42
5) runtime validates via external tool -> tool returns receipt; runtime runs sanitizer -> commit_frame(frame_42, outcome=validated, final_payload_reference=ref://frames/42/v1)
6) SDK receives commit, replaces placeholder with structured receipt object, fires onCommit callback

Edge cases and failure modes
- Commit reordering: commits can arrive out of band (after later text). Frame ids must be globally unique per response and SDKs must apply commits idempotently.
- Large payloads: for >32KB payloads server should prefer reference + incremental download rather than inline replacement. SDKs should fetch final payload via lightweight GET and verify checksum.
- Cross-tenant tool latency: quarantined frames waiting on slow downstream tools might create head-of-line issues; isolate by per-tenant concurrency limits and advertise degraded SLOs in response metadata.

Security and compliance considerations
- Quarantine is a natural place to perform additional redaction and policy checks before releasing structured outputs. Make sure quarantine store respects customer data residency and retention rules (especially for Private deployments).
- Audit logs: every transition (emit quarantined, commit, timeout/fallback) should be logged with actor metadata for compliance.

Developer experience and migration story
- Backwards compatibility: existing clients (accept_quarantine=false) continue to behave as today (immediate frames or fallback). For most customers the default remains backwards compatible.
- Migration guide: SDK vX will include helpers to opt into quarantine. Provide sample UI components (React, SwiftUI, Android) implementing placeholder -> commit transitions. Provide linting rules for server-integrated schemas.

Milestones and next steps (draft timeline)
- Discovery (2 wks): surface prioritized client apps that most need quarantine (payments, ecommerce connectors, legal). Wireframe UX patterns with solutions engineering.
- Runtime PoC (4 wks): implement quarantined frame events and local in-memory quarantine store on a subset of hosted nodes. Basic commit flow with schema validation step only.
- SDK prototypes (3 wks parallel): add onQuarantineCandidate/onCommit to JS/Swift/Kotlin SDKs + UI sample kits.
- Pilot (6 wks): run with 2 internal customers (one using tool chaining heavily) and measure commit latency and fallback rate.
- Beta (8 wks): expose to selected external teams with Console telemetry and SLA knobs.

Open questions / trade-offs (brainstorm list)
- Bandwidth vs immediacy: should we prioritize sending partial authoritative text for UX over delaying until commit? Offer per-route preferences.
- Complexity on client: how much SDK magic is acceptable (automatic patching vs explicit developer reconciliation)? Aim for small helpers, not full automation.
- Billing: do we charge for quarantined storage and commits? If so, how to communicate to customers?
- Cross-model compatibility: ensure commit/patched diffs work across model families (some models may not produce deterministic patches).
- Security: storing quarantined payloads even transiently increases attack surface; need SRE/infra signoff for storage lifecycle and encryption-at-rest.

Appendix: small notes and examples
- Quick example commit header (human readable): frame_id=42, kind=structured, schema_hint=invoice.v2, initial_confidence=0.58, timeout_ms=30000
- UX guidance: show placeholder with microcopy: "verifying results — will update shortly". Allow users to collapse or hide placeholders.
- Slack threads for follow-up: #product-hosted-api, #sdk-js, #infra-quarantine

Summary
Adaptive output quarantine is a lightweight server-side lifecycle that gives clients a predictable, observable way to handle non-authoritative structured output and tool results. It reduces brittle client heuristics, gives us a place to perform security/validation before surfacing results, and enables a smoother UX on flaky networks. Next step: align on minimal event schema and build a runtime PoC connected to JS/Swift SDK helpers.

Notes to self / TODOs
- Draft proto for quarantine events and share with infra and SDK owners (Diego + Lina)
- Spike storage TTL behaviour under peak loads (Evan)
notes_to_reviewers: This is an early draft. Look for: SDK ergonomics friction points, storage cost assumptions, and SLA knobs that product should own. If you want to pilot, ping me in #product-hosted-api or reply with the team name and workload sample.
